title: Number our days
hook: teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom
carry: establish thou the work of our hands

segments.voice: Yesterday, shiva, the week when the community comes to the mourner. Your line was none spake a word unto him. Did you call or visit? Today, a psalm that asks to learn how to count. Day seven hundred seventy-five.

"So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." That's one verse from Psalm 90, the psalm whose heading calls it a prayer of Moses, the man of God. It sounds almost like a math lesson. Count your days. But the psalm around it is about how short a human life is, and it doesn't ask for more days. It asks to count the ones there are. Today: what counting has to do with wisdom.
screen: `TEACH US TO NUMBER OUR DAYS.` → `A PRAYER OF MOSES.` → `WHY COUNT?`

segments.voice: First, God's clock. The psalm opens wide, with God before the mountains were born, and then says: "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night." Time that feels endless to us passes, for God, like one short watch. Second, the grass. People, the psalm says, are like grass: "In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth." One day, start to finish. Third, the count. The psalm puts numbers on it: seventy years, eighty if there's strength, "for it is soon cut off, and we fly away." And then, right after, comes the verse: teach us to number our days. Not to dread them, and not to bargain for more. To count them, so that we bring home a heart of wisdom. Counting is how you notice that something is limited, and noticing is how you start to treat it with care. Fourth, where it lands. The psalm doesn't end on the grass. Its last words ask for something to last: "establish thou the work of our hands." Count the days, and then let the work done in them matter. In some Jewish communities this psalm is part of the Sabbath and festival morning prayers, and it is sometimes read at funerals. In a service of praise or beside a grave, the same verse sits in the middle of it, asking for a lesson in counting.
screen: `A THOUSAND YEARS AS YESTERDAY.` · `GRASS BY EVENING.` · `SOON CUT OFF, AND WE FLY AWAY.` · `ESTABLISH THE WORK OF OUR HANDS.` · then, large: `NUMBER OUR DAYS.`

segments.voice: Count today. Not the ones left. Just this one. On each breath out, count one thing this day has already held: waking up, a cup of something warm, a voice, a stretch of quiet, a task done. If you run out, count the things still ahead before you sleep. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line, so teach us to number our days. Otherwise, just keep counting, slowly, and notice that the day is full of things. The bell holds the time.
Moses, whose psalm asks God to teach us to number our days, so that we gain a heart of wisdom. Today's word.
Your line: establish thou the work of our hands. Tonight, before you sleep, name one thing from today that you want to have counted. Day seven hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: In some Jewish communities Psalm 90 is prayed in the morning prayers of the Sabbath and festivals, and it is sometimes read at funerals; Christians read it too, in their own services.

fork.setup: the psalm has just said life is soon cut off, and we fly away. what does it ask for next?

notes: All quotations are KJV; JPS 1917 may be preferred for the Jewish voices block.

Liturgical use: Psalm 90 in Sabbath and festival morning prayers (Pesukei dezimra) and sometimes at funerals; please confirm.
Original לִמְנוֹת יָמֵינוּ and pronunciation: please verify.
Editor pass: 'Jews pray this psalm' in Sabbath and festival prayers narrowed to 'in some Jewish communities' (claims rule; rites differ), in the teach and howItsDone; the vague 'Either way' replaced.

Audit (2026-10-01): the gloss on 90:4 compared a human life to the night watch, which misreads the verse (it is the thousand years that are like a watch); rewritten. All KJV quotations confirmed; practice opener varied.
